metadata.title: Jobs vs. Prices: The Fed's Balancing Act
metadata.section: Section B: Macroeconomics, Money & Financial Conditions
metadata.visual_form: A moving dot across four zones

explanation.summary: The Phillips curve says that when unemployment is low, prices rise faster, and when unemployment is high, prices calm down. This loop plots both, month by month, since 1965. The rule holds in some periods and breaks down completely in others.
explanation.methodology: Unemployment rate from the BLS Current Population Survey (LNS14000000). Inflation is the year-over-year change in the BLS CPI-U (CUUR0000SA0).

key_findings.title: 1975: Stagflation
key_findings.description: Unemployment was 9.0% and inflation was 9.5% at the same time.
key_findings.significance: High unemployment did not stop high inflation.

key_findings.title: 1982: The Cure Hurts
key_findings.description: After the Fed raised interest rates sharply, inflation fell from a peak of 14.8% (March 1980) to 4.6%. Unemployment rose to 10.8%.
key_findings.significance: Bringing down inflation cost millions of jobs.

key_findings.title: 2022: Low Unemployment, High Inflation
key_findings.description: Inflation hit 9.1% with unemployment at only 3.6%. As of August 2026, inflation is 3.4% and unemployment 4.1%.
key_findings.significance: Inflation came down a long way without a big rise in unemployment.
